Nothing's been at that midden in weeks and something's been sleeping in the straw. Husks, said Milo. Husks. Are we going to? You're going to. Torrin looked at the shed. Nine days ago he would have looked at it and seen a shed. What he saw now, and he was pleased with himself about it, in a way he would want back within the hour, was a four foot doorway, a lintel low enough to take your teeth out, straw on a beaten earth floor, a wall of loose stone on the left that would go if you put a shoulder into it, and no light passed about six feet in. They kicked the door frame and made noise and the first husk came out into the yard light at a flat run and Wick took it across the shins with the bar and Torrin put the spike through it under the arm and it came apart into gray and it took about four seconds. The second one came out three seconds behind the first and did the same thing and lasted about as long. Torrin had a full second and a half in which he understood that he was extremely good at this. Then the third one came out of the dark of the shed, low and fast and silent, and did not come at Wick and did not come at Torrin. It went straight for the light. Milo screamed, which was correct, and did not drop the light, which was remarkable, and went over backwards with the thing on top of him. The spike went out. It went out the way a candle goes out in a draft, completely, instantly, between one heartbeat and the next, and Torrin was standing in a farmyard with a gray stone in his fist and a husk on top of Milo four feet away and he did the only thing available to a person in that situation which was to fall on it bodily with a rock in his hand. He hit it with his own fist. He hit it with the ember. He hit it four times before Wick got the bar under its chin and hauled it off and stood on it and it came apart and the gray ran out across the beaten earth of the yard and went into the seams. Milo sat up. You did, said Rook from the gate where he had not moved. Why does it go out? They were sitting on the yard wall. Rook had let them collect the ash themselves for the first time, three seams worth, which in the flat tin flask came to about two fingers and Rook had looked at it and said, a handful maybe if you sold it at a wall and don't ever let them tell you it's less. Why does it go out? Why does it go out? Torrin said again. Tell me your answer first. I don't have an answer. You have four, said Rook. You've had one a day since the bridge. Say the current one.
